doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Why traditional jazz is mostly white, and playing in an all-black band
summary: Reflections on race in Dixieland audiences and players, and his experience as the only white player in a black band.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Why is it that — I don’t know if there’s an answer to this question — but it seems that the music, the mainstream and the Dixieland is predominantly played by white players, and the audience for it too. And I sometimes wonder why.

I wish I knew. If it’s a matter of making money I can understand, because I don’t know any wealthy jazz musicians. But I don’t know lots of white musicians who’ve played blues or soul who have overseas tours and make lots of recordings. And you know I think it’s a matter of going where the money is, and I can’t blame anyone for that. I wish there were more black players, but the ones who play it tend to like, really, more modern styles — mainstream and beyond — rather than the earlier styles.

Right. I guess the Joshua Redman and Christian McBride and that, those younger players, they do standards, but then they’re more into I guess their own music, kind of breaking — I don’t know if they’re breaking ground or not.

They probably are. And I think there’s a number of musicians who play traditional jazz in concerts and tours and make recordings, but given their choice of what to play, that would not be what they want to play. They can make a certain good living doing that, but that’s not their music. And I’ve witnessed that time and again. I know a trombone player in New Orleans, Freddie Lonzo, who is one of the few black players I’ve heard who really digs into the style and likes the style and is not on the bandstand like hoping to get off soon. I wish it wasn’t that way. It’s not been that way in the past, not until well into the ‘50s and the Bebop era. I mean we look at photos of jam sessions, at Jimmy Ryan’s in the late ‘30s and ‘40s, I mean it’s a total mixture. It’s like nobody gave a second thought to that kind of thing, and it didn’t really become that way until recent time, that I can tell. I mean I like playing, I’ve played where I’ve been the only white in the band, and I’ve been the drummer, and if there’s a hot seat in an all black band, it’s the drummer. But I had a ball. And the guys liked it. I thought I’m going to play for them, I’m not going to play what I think will work here. I tried that, it failed miserably. It was a supposed traditional jazz band. And I could hear a lot of swing influence in the players, but not the older styles. The older style just didn’t work, it didn’t set them off. So I thought all right, forget those people out there who are going to give me dirty looks in the audience. I’ll just play what they want. So I laid in the rim shots and the ride cymbal, and took off. And I was accepted. And the next time I showed up they were all, “Hey, welcome back, man.” So I just play for the band, and I know the people in the audience thought well that’s not the correct set up that we want to see, what’s that guy doing there? But I was there and I just made the best of it. But I have no problem with, I mean you can’t make that a racial thing. If you make it into that, you’re going to have a very unhappy bandstand. There’s just no point in it.
